::: {.why}
One contract of one thing is not comparable to one contract of another, and the notional-to-risk conversion is where a futures book either becomes a portfolio or stays a pile of positions.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Convert a signal into a contract count via a risk target, contract multiplier and volatility estimate, and check the arithmetic end to end.
- Report the risk contribution of each instrument in your book and say whether it matches what you intended.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Do the conversion explicitly in qlib/portfolio.py: target risk per instrument, divided by the instrument's volatility in currency terms per contract, gives a contract count that must then be rounded. Rounding matters for small books and the rounding error is a real cost, so report it.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Check what you actually built: report the ex-ante risk contribution of each instrument in the combined book and compare against the equal-risk intention. Then compare the ex-post realised contributions. The gap between intended, ex-ante and realised is the thing to know about your own book.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Note the constraint a small account faces: with a fixed contract size, below a certain capital level you cannot hold a diversified futures book at all. Compute your own threshold.
:::
:::

:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Your book intends equal risk across four instruments and realises 40 percent in one. Name two causes and how you would tell them apart.
:::
